paragraphs: Training a support vector machine on a large dataset can make the amount of data processed at each step a central computational concern. This paper proposes a randomized learning algorithm that repeatedly works with randomly selected subsets of the data. Its scalability depends especially on how large those subsets need to be.

The theoretical contribution addresses that question in the context of text classification. Using ideas from random projections, the authors show that a sample size growing as O(log n) can produce a solution close to the optimum with high probability. This connects the computational shortcut to a probabilistic approximation guarantee, rather than relying only on the intuition that a small sample might be representative.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate improved scalability without loss of accuracy in the reported evaluations. Together, the theory and experiments support using small randomized subsets to make SVM learning more manageable. The near-optimality guarantee is stated for the text-classification setting, while the experimental results provide evidence about the algorithm’s practical behavior.
neurips-2007-a-randomized-algorithm-for-.tldr: Randomized training on small data subsets scales SVM learning, with a high-probability near-optimality result for text classification.

paragraphs: People can express preferences by choosing among presented items, even when the possible items vary continuously. This paper develops an active learning algorithm that uses these discrete choices to learn a continuous valuation model. The practical objective is to find something an individual values highly while keeping the number of interactions small.

The algorithm chooses each query by maximizing expected improvement. This focuses its effort on finding better items without requiring an accurate model of preferences across the entire choice space. That distinction matters because there are infinitely many possible choices, making comprehensive modeling needlessly expensive for the stated objective. The design also uses characteristics of human psychology to reduce time and cognitive burden.

The authors demonstrate effectiveness relative to related active learning methods and integrate the algorithm into a tool for digital artists choosing material-rendering parameters. In that application, preference queries guide the search for desirable settings. The work connects an adaptive statistical search strategy to an interactive task where the cost of asking a person another question is part of the problem.
neurips-2007-active-preference-learning-.tldr: An active preference learner selects choices by expected improvement to find highly valued items with fewer interactions.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes a classification method that assumes access to three sources of data: positive examples, negative examples, and an additional collection called the Universum. The central question is how a learning principle built around this extra collection relates to more familiar ways of constructing a classifier. The contribution is an analysis of a previously proposed algorithm.

The authors establish connections with Fisher discriminant analysis and oriented principal component analysis. These links place the method alongside approaches concerned with selecting informative directions in the data. They also connect it to a support vector machine operating in a projected subspace. An equivalent description uses a reduced kernel whose form depends on the data.

These alternative views help explain the algorithm through its relationship to representation and classification. The projected-subspace description and the reduced-kernel description offer two ways to understand the same connection. The paper also supplies experimental results. Its stated contribution is therefore both conceptual and empirical: it clarifies the behavior of Universum-based inference while examining the method experimentally.
neurips-2007-an-analysis-of-inference-wi.tldr: The paper explains Universum-based classification through connections to discriminant analysis, oriented PCA, and SVMs in projected spaces.

paragraphs: Neurophysiologists summarize spike activity around a stimulus using time histograms or smoother spike density functions. These summaries depend on choices about temporal resolution: histogram bin width or the width of a smoothing kernel. If those choices are relatively arbitrary, an important part of the resulting estimate rests on a manually chosen setting.

This paper develops an exact Bayesian generative approach to estimating peristimulus time histograms. A generative model provides a probabilistic account of the observed data, and Bayesian inference uses that account to estimate the response. The approach includes automatic complexity control, addressing how much detail the estimate should contain within the modeling procedure.

The authors report that their method outperforms competing approaches in their demonstration. It also supplies error bars on its predictions, so the output communicates uncertainty as well as an estimated response. These features make the contribution broader than an alternative way to divide time into bins: the method combines estimation, control of model complexity, and uncertainty reporting in one statistical framework.
neurips-2007-bayesian-binning-beats-appr.tldr: An exact Bayesian model estimates stimulus-aligned spike histograms with automatic complexity control and predictive error bars.

paragraphs: A contracting dynamical system progressively loses the influence of its starting conditions: differences between trajectories shrink exponentially until they converge to a common trajectory. This paper uses contraction theory to analyze recurrent neural networks. It derives an upper bound on recurrent connection strength that is sufficient to guarantee this behavior.

The analysis focuses on cooperative competitive networks, whose connectivity abstracts patterns of cooperation and competition observed in cortex. Such networks are believed to help shape cortical responses and select relevant signals amid distractors and noise. A contraction guarantee provides a way to reason about whether recurrent interactions will forget initial conditions, rather than preserve different trajectories indefinitely.

The authors analyze combinations of these networks using linear threshold units, then verify their analytical results in a hybrid analog and digital VLSI implementation containing spiking neurons and dynamic synapses. This connects a mathematical condition to a physical neural-network circuit. The bound supplies a sufficient condition for contraction; the abstract does not characterize it as a necessary boundary for all contracting networks.
neurips-2007-contraction-properties-of-v.tldr: Contraction theory yields a sufficient bound on recurrent connection strength, verified in a spiking-neuron hardware network.

paragraphs: Covariate shift occurs when training and test inputs follow different distributions. The paper considers correcting likelihood-based learning by weighting training contributions according to their importance for the test distribution. The required importance is the ratio of the test input density to the training input density, making accurate ratio estimation a central task.

One approach estimates both densities separately and then divides them. The authors argue that this can perform poorly, especially in high dimensions, because estimating the densities is itself difficult. They propose estimating importance directly, avoiding the need to solve those two density-estimation problems as intermediate steps.

The method also includes a model-selection procedure for choosing tuning parameters such as kernel width. This provides an objective way to tune the estimator, which the abstract identifies as an advantage over another direct importance-estimation method. Simulations illustrate the approach’s usefulness. The contribution combines a more targeted estimation problem with a way to select its settings, addressing both how importance weights are obtained and how the estimator is configured.
neurips-2007-direct-importance-estimatio.tldr: Direct density-ratio estimation with built-in model selection supports adaptation when training and test input distributions differ.

paragraphs: Discriminative clustering combines finding groups with selecting a subspace through linear discriminant analysis. Earlier empirical results favored this framework, but its iterative procedure made the relationship between these two operations difficult to understand. This paper addresses that theoretical question by showing an equivalence to kernel K-means with a particular kernel Gram matrix.

The equivalence gives a different mathematical description of the joint procedure: subspace selection and clustering can be understood through a kernel-based clustering formulation. Building on this connection, the authors introduce Discriminative K-means, or DisKmeans, together with an automatic parameter-estimation procedure. The result turns the theoretical relationship into an algorithm for performing both tasks.

The paper also develops a nonlinear kernel extension and shows how learning a kernel matrix within a convex set of specified candidates can enter the clustering formulation. It analyzes relationships with other clustering methods and evaluates the theories and algorithms on benchmark datasets. The central contribution is a unified explanation and algorithmic development of a framework whose favorable empirical behavior had previously been better understood than its internal relationships.
neurips-2007-discriminative-k-means-for-.tldr: An equivalence with kernel K-means explains joint discriminant subspace selection and clustering and motivates the DisKmeans algorithm.

paragraphs: In a controlled stochastic system with only partial observations, the current observation alone may not summarize everything useful from the past. A state representation must retain sufficient information from that history. Predictive representations of state approach this problem by describing state through statistics of future observations.

This paper introduces an exponential family predictive representation. Its state consists of changing parameters of an exponential family distribution over a sequence of n future observations. That design connects predictive state representations with probabilistic modeling tools for high-dimensional distributions, including graphical models and maximum entropy models. The representation therefore provides a route for applying those modeling techniques to dynamical systems.

The authors present maximum-likelihood parameter learning and explain how several existing approximate inference methods apply. They evaluate the model through reinforcement learning, directly examining its control performance. This evaluation ties the representation to its intended operational use: supporting decisions in a partially observed system. The contribution combines a definition of predictive state with learning and inference machinery drawn from probabilistic modeling.
neurips-2007-exponential-family-predicti.tldr: Exponential family predictive states connect partially observed dynamical systems to probabilistic density models, learning, and approximate inference.

paragraphs: Intermittent web failures can be difficult to diagnose because observed request problems do not directly identify their causes. This paper uses Bayesian inference to reason about possible faults from observations. Its target problem involves 10,000 possible faults and 100,000 observations, with inference required to finish in less than a second.

The authors meet that computational requirement by combining a variational approximation, a mean-field approximation, and stochastic gradient descent on a variational cost function. These components make the inference problem tractable enough for the required speed. The contribution centers on bringing probabilistic diagnosis to a scale and latency requirement that would otherwise make it difficult to use.

The method is applied to a time series of anomalous HTTP requests from a real web service. The reported inference speed is sufficient to analyze logs containing billions of entries within hours. This connects the subsecond inference requirement to a larger operational workload: fast individual diagnostic computations make it possible to process an extensive history of service observations.
neurips-2007-fast-variational-inference-.tldr: Combined variational and mean-field approximations enable subsecond Bayesian fault inference for large-scale web-service diagnosis.

paragraphs: Combining biological measurements creates data whose parts can behave differently. Different measurement sources may have different missing-value patterns, noise levels, and effective dimensionalities. This paper introduces heterogeneous component analysis, or HCA, to extract underlying factors while accounting for this block structure.

HCA is a linear, block-wise sparse Bayesian form of principal component analysis. Its probabilistic model assigns residual variance terms by block, allowing noise characteristics to differ between sources. It also treats the factor-loading matrix in a Bayesian way with block-wise sparsity. This structure allows extracted factors to reflect how different groups of measurements participate in the underlying components.

The authors investigate multiple algorithms implementing the HCA concept. These algorithms extract components shared across blocks as well as components specific to an individual block. Simulations using toy and bioinformatics data support the usefulness of this structured factorization approach. The significance is the ability to distinguish common variation from source-specific variation while representing differences among measurement blocks within the same feature-extraction model.
neurips-2007-heterogeneous-component-ana.tldr: Heterogeneous component analysis extracts shared and block-specific factors while modeling differences among measurement sources.

paragraphs: Dimensionality reduction seeks a lower-dimensional representation of data that may lie along a nonlinear manifold. The motivation here is that existing projection methods can lose substantial precision during that transformation. The paper introduces Manifold Sculpting as an iterative way to reduce dimensionality while addressing the accuracy of the resulting representation.

Its central mechanism simulates surface tension within local neighborhoods. This makes neighborhood-level structure part of the process that progressively reshapes the data into fewer dimensions. The method is described as iterative, so the dimensionality reduction develops through repeated adjustments. The surface-tension idea supplies the organizing principle for those adjustments.

Experiments on generated and natural datasets show more accurate results than existing algorithms in the reported comparisons. The paper also states that Manifold Sculpting can benefit from prior dimensionality-reduction efforts, giving earlier processing a role in the approach. The stated findings support an iterative, locally guided transformation as a useful alternative for obtaining accurate nonlinear representations, with evidence spanning both constructed data and naturally occurring datasets.
neurips-2007-iterative-non-linear-dimens.tldr: Manifold Sculpting iteratively reduces dimensionality using simulated local surface tension and reports improved accuracy on generated and natural data.

paragraphs: Human knowledge often consists of connected systems of beliefs about relationships, described as intuitive theories. This paper proposes that such theories are mentally represented in a logical language. It further proposes that a theory’s subjective complexity depends on the length of its representation in that language.

The representation-length idea connects two activities: learning a theory from observed relations and using it to infer relations that have not been observed. Under this account, complexity is tied to how a theory is expressed, making the choice of mental representation central to the explanation. The same proposed measure helps account for both acquiring knowledge and extending it beyond the available examples.

The authors describe two experiments testing the approach and report that it explains human learning and reasoning better than an approach developed by Goodman. This provides comparative evidence for the proposed account in those experiments. The contribution is a unified hypothesis about representation and complexity that links relational theory learning with inductive reasoning, rather than treating them as unrelated abilities.
neurips-2007-learning-and-using-relation.tldr: A logical representation-length account of intuitive theories explains relational learning and inference better than a comparison approach in two experiments.

paragraphs: Web search ranking requires ordering results by relevance, while classification predicts relevance categories. This paper connects the two by formulating ranking through multiple classification and multiple ordinal classification. These formulations lead to computationally tractable learning algorithms and provide a classification-based route to optimizing relevance orderings.

The motivation comes from discounted cumulative gain, or DCG, a ranking-quality measure. The authors establish that perfect classifications produce perfect DCG scores and that classification errors bound DCG errors. They then use expected relevance to turn predicted class probabilities into ranking scores. A gradient boosting tree algorithm learns those probabilities.

Large-scale evaluations show that the approach can improve normalized DCG relative to LambdaRank and a regression-based ranker. The paper also presents an efficient implementation of the boosting tree algorithm. Its contribution links a theoretical relationship between classification and ranking errors to a practical scoring procedure. The experimental findings support this route to ranking quality on the evaluated datasets without implying that every reduction in classification error must improve every ranking.
neurips-2007-mcrank-learning-to-rank-usi.tldr: McRank learns relevance-class probabilities with boosted trees and converts them into ranking scores using expected relevance.

paragraphs: This paper treats large software repositories as material for statistical learning. The authors first build infrastructure to crawl, parse, and store open-source code automatically. One collection includes 4,632 Java projects from SourceForge and Apache, exceeding 38 million lines of code and involving 9,250 developers.

Statistical analyses reveal robust power-law patterns in package, source-line-count, and method-call distributions. The authors then apply unsupervised probabilistic author-topic models to discover topics in code and estimate relationships between topics, words, and developers. These distributions summarize program functionality and developer activities, while providing a statistical basis for analyzing developer similarity and competence, topic scattering, and document tangling.

For software retrieval, the authors combine textual content with structural information captured by CodeRank. They report an AUC of 0.86, approximately 10–30% better than earlier approaches using text alone. The work therefore connects collection infrastructure, exploratory statistical analysis, and learned representations to a concrete retrieval improvement. It shows how repository-scale code analysis can support both descriptions of software activity and an applied software-engineering task.
neurips-2007-mining-internet-scale-softw.tldr: Repository-scale statistical models summarize code and developers, while combining text with CodeRank structure improves software retrieval.

paragraphs: Multiple-instance learning uses labels attached to groups of examples, called bags. A negative bag is assumed to contain only negative instances, while a positive bag must contain at least one positive instance. This creates an information gap: a positive group label does not reveal which of its members is responsible for that label.

The paper introduces an active learning framework that lets a learner request labels for selected instances inside positive bags. This fits situations where group labels are cheap to obtain but individual labels are possible and costly. The authors develop a method that learns from both levels of labeling and propose two query-selection strategies motivated by the multiple-instance setting.

Experiments in content-based image recognition and text classification show that instance labels can significantly improve a basic multiple-instance learner’s performance. The result supports selectively adding finer-grained supervision to an existing collection of bag labels. The approach matters because it makes the location of labeling effort part of the learning procedure, focusing attention on instances whose status remains unresolved by their group labels.
neurips-2007-multiple-instance-active-le.tldr: Selectively labeling instances within positive bags can improve multiple-instance learning while combining coarse and fine supervision.

paragraphs: This paper proposes an online algorithm for learning linear-threshold functions, which classify examples according to which side of a linear boundary they occupy. The algorithm combines second-order information about the data with the logarithmic behavior associated with multiplicative and dual-norm learning algorithms. The goal is to bring these properties together efficiently.

An initial theoretical analysis suggests an interpretation in terms of an ordinary Perceptron operating on transformed examples. Under that interpretation, the transformation improves margin properties, meaning the examples have a more favorable relationship to the separating boundary. The authors present this as a suggested view of the algorithm, rather than a fully established general explanation.

Experiments across diverse domains compare the procedure with first-order, second-order, additive, and multiplicative Perceptron methods. The authors report that it appears to generalize well and converges faster than the corresponding multiplicative baselines. The contribution is thus an algorithmic combination supported by preliminary theoretical insight and empirical comparisons, with the stated speed finding specifically referring to those multiplicative baseline algorithms.
neurips-2007-on-higher-order-perceptron-.tldr: A new online Perceptron variant combines second-order statistics with multiplicative-style behavior and converges faster than corresponding multiplicative baselines in experiments.

paragraphs: Boosting builds a predictor from base classifiers. This paper studies algorithms that make a single pass over a set of those classifiers. In the setting of diverse base classifiers, the authors analyze a one-pass algorithm whose guarantee matches the strongest previously proved for boosting, while being much faster than earlier approaches.

The paper also investigates whether a boosting procedure should use every available base classifier. It constructs a random source of examples where a selective variant of AdaBoost, which skips poor classifiers, can outperform the standard version by an exponential factor. This is a result for the exhibited source, establishing that rejecting some classifiers can have a substantial benefit under suitable conditions.

Experiments on Reuters and synthetic data show that one-pass boosting can substantially improve the accuracy of Naive Bayes. Selective boosting sometimes provides an additional improvement. The theoretical and experimental findings address complementary questions: whether a single pass can retain a strong guarantee, and whether choosing which classifiers to include can further improve the resulting predictor.
neurips-2007-one-pass-boosting-719cb6855.tldr: One-pass boosting retains a strong theoretical guarantee, while selectively skipping poor classifiers can provide further benefits.

paragraphs: This paper addresses online learning in Markov decision processes with continuous states and actions. Such a setting calls for learning about a system while interacting with it, rather than working only with a finite list of possible situations and choices. The authors provide a provably efficient algorithm using a model-based approach.

The main technical connection is to a special form of online linear regression. The authors show that this regression method enables learning MDPs whose dynamics have a linear parameterization, potentially using kernels. This places learning the system’s dynamics at the center of the reinforcement-learning procedure and gives regression a role in obtaining an efficiency guarantee.

The result builds on earlier work by Kearns and Singh for finite-state MDPs. The abstract also states that the approach applies beyond the linear setting to other classes of continuous MDPs. The significance is a bridge from efficient learning in finite systems to structured continuous systems. The explicit regression-based result concerns linearly parameterized dynamics, while the broader approach has further stated applicability.
neurips-2007-online-linear-regression-an.tldr: A specialized online regression method enables provably efficient model-based learning of continuous MDPs with linearly parameterized dynamics.

paragraphs: Barn owl sound localization is commonly explained by comparing auditory cues with stored templates. These matching models can explain aspects of neural responses, but spatial ambiguity poses a behavioral problem: the same cues can leave uncertainty about direction. The paper asks how owls nevertheless localize accurately near the center of gaze.

The authors compare two estimators. Maximum likelihood provides a way to examine localization based on cue matching. Maximum a posteriori estimation adds a prior that favors directions near the center of gaze. This comparison tests whether including that directional preference helps account for behavior that the cue information alone does not explain.

The maximum-likelihood estimator fails to reproduce the owl’s behavior, whereas the maximum-a-posteriori estimator matches it. The authors interpret this as evidence that standard cue matching is insufficient for explaining the behavior. Their Bayesian model offers a framework for further analysis and generates behavioral predictions. The finding supports the explanatory value of a gaze-centered prior without establishing that the owl implements this particular estimator.
neurips-2007-optimal-models-of-sound-loc.tldr: A Bayesian estimator favoring directions near the center of gaze matches owl localization behavior that a maximum-likelihood cue-matching model cannot reproduce.

paragraphs: Semantic memory includes knowledge of facts and relationships between concepts, including relationships that were never directly taught. This paper connects that ability to a mechanism from models of episodic memory: retrieving a representation of temporal context that changes gradually over time. The question is whether retrieved context can help organize broader knowledge.

The authors show that this mechanism supports the formation of a global memory space reflecting relationships among previously learned items. When new information enters that space, it takes on relationships to other items even when those connections have not been explicitly learned. They demonstrate this effect for structures with ring and two-dimensional sheet topologies.

The model is also trained on a large collection of synonym pairs to examine a more realistic semantic setting. Retrieved context enables it to infer relationships between pairs that have not yet been presented. The contribution links a temporal-context mechanism associated with remembering episodes to the emergence of semantic structure, showing how individual learning experiences can become part of a more interconnected representation.
neurips-2007-retrieved-context-and-the-d.tldr: Retrieved temporal context helps a memory model build global semantic structure and infer relationships that were not explicitly taught.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning draws on both labeled and unlabeled examples, while multitask learning connects related prediction tasks. This paper combines these ideas in a framework that jointly learns multiple classifiers. Each classifier is associated with its own partially labeled data manifold, giving the framework both within-task data structure and relationships across tasks to use.

A soft-sharing prior couples the classifiers’ parameters while allowing them to differ. Unlabeled examples contribute through neighborhoods defined by a Markov random walk on a graph representing each manifold. This gives unlabeled data a structural role in learning: the graph and its random-walk neighborhoods help determine how the classifier uses the organization of examples.

Experiments on real datasets show significant generalization improvements over semi-supervised single-task learning and supervised multitask learning. These comparisons indicate that the combination can provide benefits beyond either using unlabeled data separately for each task or sharing information using only supervised learning. The reported finding supports integrating neighborhood structure and parameter sharing within a common learning framework.
neurips-2007-semi-supervised-multitask-l.tldr: Joint classifiers combine graph-based use of unlabeled data with soft parameter sharing, improving generalization in real-data experiments.

paragraphs: A variable-order Markov model allows different predictions to depend on different amounts of preceding context. This paper introduces a nonparametric Bayesian method for estimating such processes with a theoretically unbounded order. It directly infers the hidden dependency order associated with each symbol, making context length part of the inference problem.

The construction extends a stick-breaking prior vertically along trees of infinite depth associated with a hierarchical Chinese restaurant process. This provides a probabilistic mechanism for working with different depths of historical dependence. The infinite-order formulation concerns the range of dependencies the model can represent, while the inferred orders determine how that flexibility is used for observed symbols.

Experiments on natural-language character and word sequences show performance comparable to an exponentially large full-order model, with substantially better time and space efficiency. The result suggests that inferring variable dependency orders can retain useful modeling capacity without the same computational burden. The authors also anticipate an extension to variable-order hierarchical clustering of general data, presenting that extension as an expectation.
neurips-2007-the-infinite-markov-model-0.tldr: A Bayesian variable-order Markov model infers context lengths and achieves comparable sequence performance to a much larger full-order model.

paragraphs: Online linear optimization requires choosing a decision each round while facing an unknown, changing linear cost. This paper compares two feedback settings. Full information reveals the cost function after the decision, while bandit feedback reveals only the cost actually incurred. The price of bandit information measures the gap between the best achievable regrets under these settings.

The authors present convergence rates and a bandit algorithm whose regret has square-root dependence on the time horizon. This improves the time dependence over previous nontrivial bounds, which had a two-thirds power or worse. Comparing the presented upper bounds gives a factor of the ambient dimension between bandit and full-information regret, quantifying the cost of reduced feedback.

The paper also establishes lower bounds on the information gap and conjectures its correct dimensional order. These distinguish the performance achieved by the algorithm from the remaining question of the exact gap. Efficient implementation is shown for particular settings of interest, including path planning and Markov decision problems, connecting the regret analysis to structured decision tasks.
neurips-2007-the-price-of-bandit-informa.tldr: A new bandit optimization algorithm improves regret’s time dependence and bounds the cost of observing only incurred losses.

paragraphs: The usefulness of unlabeled data depends on assumptions about how observations and classes relate. A well-understood setting assumes an identifiable mixture distribution in which each class corresponds to a pure component. Earlier analysis of that setting found regimes where labeled examples become exponentially more valuable than unlabeled ones.

This paper investigates what happens when the mixture description is only approximate. The underlying data distribution can be modeled by an identifiable mixture, but the fit is imperfect. This intermediate setting retains some structure from mixture models while acknowledging that a practical model, such as a Gaussian mixture, may not exactly describe the data.

The contribution is an analysis of how the roles of labeled and unlabeled examples depend on the amount of model imperfection. This shifts attention from whether unlabeled data is useful in an idealized model to how that usefulness changes when the model is inaccurate. It connects semi-supervised learning theory to a setting where the modeling assumption is informative without being exactly true.
neurips-2007-the-value-of-labeled-and-un.tldr: The paper analyzes how imperfect mixture models change the relative value of labeled and unlabeled training examples.

paragraphs: Transfer learning aims to reduce the examples needed for a new problem by using information from earlier problems. A central difficulty is defining how tasks are related and how much information should pass between them. This paper proposes conditional Kolmogorov complexity as a measure of how much information one task contains about another.

The idea connects relatedness to how compactly one task can be described given another. In a sequential Bayesian setting, the authors show how existing theory supplies both a measure of relatedness and a principle for transferring an appropriate amount of information. They further argue that, in a precise formal sense, no other reasonable transfer method can do much better, and sequential transfer is justified within that theoretical account.

The authors also develop a practical approximation and apply it to transfer among eight arbitrarily chosen UCI databases. This connects the formal proposal to an implementable procedure. The abstract’s strong claims concern the theoretical setting; the empirical work evaluates an approximation of that method rather than establishing the same formal properties for every practical transfer application.
neurips-2007-transfer-learning-using-kol.tldr: Conditional Kolmogorov complexity provides a formal account of task relatedness and information transfer, alongside a practical approximation.
